title: Wearable Technology to Garner the Perspective of Dementia Family Caregivers.
authors: Matthews JT, Campbell GB, Hunsaker AE, Klinger J, Mecca LP, Hu L, et al.
finding_for_nametags: A prototype camera system worn by the family caregiver, not the person with dementia, captured image and voice data at home so nurses and other providers could see the behaviors and interactions the caregiver finds difficult, in a pilot with 18 caregiving dyads. It shows only that a worn camera and microphone have been used inside dementia households; the abstract reports no usability, privacy or reaction results and nothing about recognizing people, so it tests no Nametags feature or tension.
method_and_sample: descriptive report of a prototype with case scenarios, from a pilot feasibility study of 18 caregiving dyads
limitation: A descriptive article with illustrative scenarios and no outcome data in the abstract, and only the abstract could be read.
supporting_sentence: The current article describes a prototype wearable camera system used to gather image and voice data from the caregiver's perspective in a pilot feasibility intervention study conducted with 18 caregiving dyads.
note: Full text not read: the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint for PMC4814293 returned HTTP 500 on three tries between 00:49 and 00:54 EDT; the record marks it free to read but not open access (isOpenAccess N), so the abstract in the Europe PMC record was used. Same group as paper 12 (MED:26288888): five shared authors and a caregiver-worn camera system in both (18 dyads here, 9 there); the abstracts do not say whether the samples overlap, so do not count the two as independent evidence.

title: Design, development, and use of conversational agents in rehabilitation for adults with brain-related neurological conditions: a scoping review.
authors: Hocking J, Oster C, Maeder A, Lange B
finding_for_nametags: A scoping review found 11 papers on conversational agents for adults with brain conditions (7 aimed at people with dementia alone or in mixed groups), all at an early stage with samples of 1 to 33, no effectiveness testing and safety considered in only two, so there is no published evidence yet that a voice assistant like Nova helps people with dementia. None of the purposes the papers reported was identifying people, which is Nova's job, and the authors ask future studies to define safety issues and clinician oversight, which product.md does not describe for Nova.
method_and_sample: scoping review of 11 papers (7 prototypes); MEDLINE, Scopus, ProQuest, Web of Science and gray literature, no date limit, English only
limitation: Only the abstract was read, and the review covers few, small, heterogeneous studies with no effectiveness or health outcomes, so it shows a gap rather than evidence for or against Nova.
note: No pmcid; abstract from the Europe PMC record, whose only full-text link is a subscription DOI. The abstract says nothing about an agent disclosing that it is an AI, so it does not inform tension 2. Reported purposes: more daily conversation (4), reminiscence (2), and one each for anxiety management and education, Parkinson disease education, recording the user's voice, monitoring well-being, and building rapport before task prompts; one study reported clinician oversight.

title: Usability of a Wearable Camera System for Dementia Family Caregivers.
authors: Matthews JT, Lingler JH, Campbell GB, Hunsaker AE, Hu L, Pires BR, et al.
finding_for_nametags: When family caregivers wore a camera system at home for 3 to 7 days to record difficult behaviors for health care providers, they judged its benefits worth the invasion of privacy beforehand, their privacy concerns did not change significantly after wear, and they found it easy to learn but cumbersome and obtrusive. That is small, indirect support for a worn camera around a person with dementia: the privacy judgment was the wearers' own, and nothing here tests a person with dementia wearing the camera or other residents and staff as bystanders (tension 3).
method_and_sample: usability study, 9 caregiving dyads (persons with dementia mean MMSE 17.33), 3 to 7 days of caregiver wear, 140 hours recorded
limitation: Nine dyads, a caregiver-worn device and only the abstract read: the privacy result is the wearers' own rating, and the abstract gives no figures for the reactions of the persons with dementia.
supporting_sentence: Prior to using the system, CGs assessed its benefits to be worth the invasion of privacy; post-wear privacy concerns did not differ significantly.
note: Full text not read: fullTextXML for PMC4545579 returned HTTP 500 on three tries between 00:49 and 00:54 EDT; the record marks it free in Europe PMC (isOpenAccess N) and lists an open-access PDF on the publisher site via Unpaywall, but the rules here allow only the Europe PMC endpoint or the abstract, so the abstract was used. Other abstract facts: 79 salient events in 140 hours, and 'Few negative reactions by PWDs were reported or evident in resulting video.' Same group as paper 10 (MED:26468655); do not count them as independent.

title: A Web-Based Mobile App With a Smartwatch to Support Social Engagement in Persons With Memory Loss: Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
authors: McCarron HR, Zmora R, Gaugler JE
finding_for_nametags: In a 6-month pilot trial with 48 people with memory loss, prior art very close to Nametags (a phone that recognized enrolled faces and showed the person's name and relationship on a smartwatch) had no significant effect on quality of social interaction or quality of life, and most users interviewed did not find it useful. Their reasons bear on Nametags' family enrollment and look-alike-relative risk: enrolling felt awkward, so many families enrolled only people they knew well, often people the wearer already remembered, and users reported failures in some lighting, recognition slower than the wearer's own question, and a son confused with a son-in-law.
method_and_sample: pilot randomized controlled trial, 48 people with memory loss (20 app, 28 usual care) with caregivers, 6 months, plus 13 phone interviews; Minnesota, USA
limitation: Small and underpowered (not planned as a pilot in advance), outcomes mostly reported by caregivers, no record of how much the app was used, and a sample that included mild cognitive impairment and self-reported memory concerns.
supporting_sentence: The absence of empirical intervention effects is supported by the qualitative analysis, which revealed that the majority of participants did not find the SSA useful.
note: Read in full. More verbatim support: 'Consequently, the individuals they enrolled were often people that the person with memory loss did not have trouble remembering.' | 'Marge (caregiver, age 67) mentioned that the software could not distinguish her son from her son-in-law, both of whom were bald and had beards but otherwise had little physical resemblance.' | 'She said that by the time the SSA recognized the face, her husband had already asked her who the person was.' Users asked for something like the Nametags design, untested here: 'Participants suggested replacing the watch with an earpiece.' and 'Instead of the phone, they recommended a lapel pin, brooch, pendant, or necklace with a camera.' Other points: mean feasibility and utility 3.11 at 3 months and 3.10 at 6 months on a 1 to 5 scale (neutral); some caregivers reported agitation, frustration and extra burden; a few found the phone worn around the neck conspicuous and stigmatizing; one caregiver said the only settings where it could help (an adult day service, a dementia chorus) already used name tags. People with memory loss needed a SLUMS score of 20 or higher (capacity to give verbal consent). Face only: nothing here tests voice recognition, so it cannot say whether voice-first presence avoids the lighting and delay failures. Funded by a National Institute on Aging grant to the developer; the authors report no financial interest in it.

title: Recognition of familiar people with a mobile cloud architecture for Alzheimer patients.
authors: Fardoun HM, Mashat AA, Ramirez Castillo J
finding_for_nametags: Earlier prior art for Nametags: photos taken with a smartwatch went to face recognition in the cloud and details about the recognized person came back to the watch; the authors report correct results (no figures in the abstract) but usability problems for patients with dementia in reading the small screen and taking a proper photo. Nametags' spoken announcement and hands-free glasses camera skip both steps by design (not tested here), but its context card is still text to read, and the cloud design is the same choice as the DEPLOY.md server, whose privacy this abstract does not discuss.
method_and_sample: system architecture and prototype tested in a real-life scenario; sample size not given in the abstract
limitation: Only the abstract was readable, and it gives no accuracy figures, sample size or test conditions, so the claim of correct results cannot be weighed.
supporting_sentence: However, when being targeted to patients with dementia some usability problems appeared, such as difficulties to read information in a small screen or take a proper photo.
note: No pmcid; abstract from the Europe PMC record, whose only full-text link is a subscription DOI. Rated high as prior art for the same idea (recognizing familiar people for Alzheimer patients and sending their details to a wearable), not for strength of evidence. The abstract says it targets medium-advanced stages and claims benefits for daily life and self-esteem without reporting data.
